title: Monaco Company: correcting a temporary bookkeeper's journal errors and depreciating office equipment
participant_role: Senior accountant at Monaco Company returning from time off
judge_role: Manager of Monaco Company who wants the bookkeeping errors corrected and explained
scenario:
You are to assume the role of the senior accountant at MONACO COMPANY. The manager of the company (participant) wants you to correct journal entries and errors made in your absence.

For the past few weeks, a temporary employee has been filling in as bookkeeper. When you returned from time off, you discovered the following errors were made in the journals. All incorrect entries were posted.

1. A payment on account of $830 to a creditor was debited to Accounts Payable $380 and credited to Cash $380.
2. The purchase of supplies on account for $500 was debited to Equipment $50 and credited to Accounts Payable $50.
3. A $400 withdrawal of cash by the manager for personal use was debited to Salaries Expense $400 and credited to Cash $400.
4. The purchase of $1,200 of office equipment on account, with a three-year useful life and no residual value, was debited to Office Supplies and credited to Accounts Payable.

You have a meeting with the manager (judge) to discuss the preliminary accounting numbers and the errors that need to be fixed. You will prepare the correct journal entries and fix the errors and explain them to the manager (judge). You will also prepare any adjusting entries necessary for the office equipment.

You will present the information to the manager (judge) in a role-play to take place in the manager's (judge's) office. The manager (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the manager's (judge's) questions, the manager (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: How do correcting entries differ from adjusting entries?
Of the errors that were identified in the case, which ones would have affected the accounting equation with regards to income if they went undetected?

solution.overview: A strong answer compares each wrong entry with the correct entry and records one correcting entry for the difference: Accounts Payable/Cash $450 for the transposed payment, Supplies $500 against Equipment $50 and Accounts Payable $450, Drawings against Salaries Expense $400, and Office Equipment against Office Supplies $1,200. It then records the adjusting entry for one year of straight-line depreciation on the equipment ($1,200 / 3 = $400) and explains how each error would have distorted the accounting equation and net income.

answer: Error 1: payment was $830 but only $380 was recorded (digits transposed); both Accounts Payable and Cash are overstated by $450 (each was reduced by $450 too little), so debit Accounts Payable $450 and credit Cash $450
Error 2: supplies of $500 were recorded as Equipment of $50; debit Supplies $500, credit Equipment $50 (to remove the wrong debit) and credit Accounts Payable $450 (to bring the liability up to $500)
Error 3: an owner withdrawal was booked as an expense; debit Drawings $400 and credit Salaries Expense $400 so equity is reduced through drawings, not through net income
Error 4: a long-term asset was booked as supplies; debit Office Equipment $1,200 and credit Office Supplies $1,200 (Accounts Payable was correct)
Approach for each: write the wrong entry, write the correct entry, then journalize the difference

by_task.task: Adjusting entry for the office equipment
answer: Straight-line depreciation: (cost $1,200 - residual value $0) / 3 years = $400 per year
Debit Depreciation Expense, Equipment $400 and credit Accumulated Depreciation, Equipment $400
Accumulated Depreciation is a contra-asset, so the equipment shows at book value $1,200 - $400 = $800 after year one
If the equipment was owned for only part of the year, prorate: $400 x months owned / 12
Error 1 overstated both assets (Cash) and liabilities (Accounts Payable) by $450; the equation still balanced but both sides were wrong
Error 2 understated assets by $450 net (Supplies too low by $500, Equipment too high by $50) and understated liabilities by $450
Error 3 overstated expenses by $400, so net income and therefore equity through income were understated, while drawings were understated by $400; total equity was correct but for the wrong reason
Error 4 misclassified $1,200 within assets and, if undetected, depreciation of $400 would never have been recorded, overstating both assets and net income

journal_entries.description: Correct error 1: payment on account recorded as $380 instead of $830
Correct error 2: $500 supplies on account recorded as $50 equipment
Correct error 3: manager's $400 withdrawal recorded as salaries expense
Correct error 4: $1,200 office equipment recorded as office supplies
Adjusting entry: one year of straight-line depreciation on office equipment

calculations.label: Error 2 correction amounts
steps: Supplies should be $500, recorded $0: debit Supplies $500
Equipment should be $0, recorded $50: credit Equipment $50
Accounts Payable should be $500, recorded $50: credit Accounts Payable $500 - $50 = $450

calculations.label: Annual straight-line depreciation on office equipment

judge_question_answers.question: How do correcting entries differ from adjusting entries?
answer: Correcting entries are not a required part of the accounting cycle; adjusting entries are made every period before the statements are prepared
Correcting entries may be made at any time an error is found; adjusting entries are made at the end of the period
Correcting entries may affect any combination of accounts; adjusting entries always affect one income statement account and one balance sheet account

judge_question_answers.question: Of the errors that were identified in the case, which ones would have affected the accounting equation with regards to income if they went undetected?
answer: Transaction 3: the $400 withdrawal was recorded as Salaries Expense, so net income would have been understated by $400

Transaction 4 arguably too: with the $1,200 sitting in Office Supplies instead of Equipment, depreciation would likely never have been calculated, overstating net income by $400 (and if the supplies were instead expensed, net income would be understated)
Transactions 1 and 2 involve only assets and liabilities, so they would not change net income

key_concepts.definition: A journal entry that fixes an error already posted; find the difference between the wrong entry and the right entry and record that difference.
An end-of-period entry that updates accounts for items like depreciation, supplies used or accrued expenses; it always touches one income statement account and one balance sheet account.
Reversing digits when recording an amount, such as $380 for $830; the difference is always divisible by 9.
Cash or assets the owner takes for personal use; recorded in Drawings, which reduces equity directly and is never an expense.
Supplies are used up quickly and are a current asset; equipment is a long-term asset that provides benefits for years and is depreciated.
Property or equipment with a useful life over one year; its cost is spread over its life through depreciation instead of being expensed at once.
Depreciation per year = (Cost - Residual value) / Useful life in years; here ($1,200 - $0) / 3 = $400.
A contra-asset account that collects all depreciation recorded on an asset; Cost - Accumulated depreciation = Book value.
The estimated amount an asset is worth at the end of its useful life; zero here.
Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity; every entry, including corrections, must keep it in balance.
Paying a creditor for a purchase made earlier on credit: debit Accounts Payable, credit Cash.
